description: Hi! I'm a high school junior leading a team for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge on the "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" project. We are building a web app that unifies satellite thermal data into fire activity calendars for emergency responders. We speak English and are looking for teammates into web dev, data analysis, UI design, or storytelling to help us build it—reach out to jo
summary: We built a burn calendar that joins two NASA satellite fire records, MODIS and VIIRS, so they can be compared. The satellites count fires differently. VIIRS has smaller pixels, so it picks up about 2.4 times more hotspots than MODIS, and putting the records side by side makes it look like fires jumped in 2012 when they didn’t. We started with Brazil as a test case. We removed weak detections, matched VIIRS to MODIS’s 1 km size, and divided VIIRS by a scale factor from the years both were flying. Then we tested it on years it hadn’t seen (2019 to 2025), and the monthly error was about 13%. A one-day check around the world showed the factor is different on each continent, so we moved on to worldwide data for one full year (2023) and fit a separate factor for each continent. Our web app lets a user pick an area and dates, see a year-by-month fire calendar, compare a month to the usual median, and download a CSV. This matters because MODIS is near the end of its life, and emergency managers need one steady record to see which months burn most and when something is unusual.
details:
The project joins two NASA fire records, MODIS and VIIRS, into one record that can be compared across time. We downloaded fire detections from NASA FIRMS and kept only the ones the satellite was fairly sure about and that were vegetation fires. VIIRS sees smaller pixels (375 m vs 1 km), so we matched it to MODIS’s size by keeping one detection per 1 km box per day. We then counted hotspots in 0.25 degree grid squares. For the years both satellites were flying, we compared monthly totals and found VIIRS counts about 2.4 times more in Brazil, so we divided VIIRS by that number. We use MODIS before 2012 and the adjusted VIIRS after, so no fire is counted twice. The web app lets a user pick an area and dates, shows a year-by-month fire calendar, compares each month to the usual median, and lets them download a CSV.

MODIS is getting old and VIIRS is replacing it, so we want fire history to stay usable after the switch. We hope it helps with early warning, planning, and tracking changes in fire seasons.

We used Python (pandas, numpy, geopandas, matplotlib, pyarrow) in Google Colab, GitHub for the code, and NASA FIRMS for the data (MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP). We also used Claude, to help write and explain some code.

Instead of matching individual fire pixels between satellites, we compared grid counts, which is simpler and holds up better. We also found the satellites’ ratio changes by region, so we tested Brazil first and then calibrated each continent on its own using a year of worldwide data. The color scales are colorblind-friendly.

The two satellites use different confidence scales, so we mapped both to low, nominal and high. We removed non-vegetation heat sources like volcanoes. Only one MODIS satellite flew in 2001, so early counts may be low. The VIIRS/MODIS ratio drifted a little in 2024 and 2025, so one factor slightly underestimates recent peaks. We checked the method on years it never saw instead of only the years it was built on. We used standard-quality data where possible, because near-real-time data gets replaced later. The Suomi-NPP satellite stopped its data on November 2, 2026, so future work should calibrate NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. We also couldn’t download the whole world’s history in the time we had, so the worldwide part uses one year.
